DOI 10.1177/0018720810376055; open copy: https://depositonce.tu-berlin.de/items/0c787d91-6021-480b-a333-009e0d1d0092/full. (2) Goddard, K., Roudsari, A., & Wyatt, J. C. (2012). Automation bias: a systematic review of frequency, effect mediators, and mitigators. J Am Med Inform Assoc, 19(1), 121-127 (online 16 June 2011). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3240751/
source_tier: Peer-reviewed (both: a literature review with a theoretical model, and a systematic review)

Goddard et al.: PMC page opened, but through an automated summariser, so the abstract and results below are summary-level, not the full text read line by line. Neither source was verified against the PDF.
sponsor_and_incentive: Goddard et al.: 'This review was carried out as part of ongoing PhD research funded by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council.' No competing interests listed. Parasuraman and Manzey: funding not seen in the abstract-level material [uncertain].
exact_quotes: Only short fragments, as returned by the fetch tool, and not checked against the PDF. Parasuraman and Manzey (abstract): complacency 'cannot be overcome with simple practice' (also attributed in the abstract: appears in novices and experts, and training or instructions do not prevent automation bias). Goddard et al. (abstract): 'the tendency to over-rely on automation'; 'a failure to recognize the new errors that CDSS can introduce'. Fragments are from tool output, so treat exact wording as [uncertain] until the PDFs are opened.
date_and_recency: Parasuraman and Manzey: 2010, Human Factors 52(3). Goddard et al.: published online June 2011, issue Jan-Feb 2012. Goddard et al. screened 13,821 papers and included 74; collection window not seen [uncertain]. Both are 14+ years old and predate LLM agents.
key_claims: Parasuraman and Manzey: complacency (reduced monitoring) and automation bias (over-reliance on advice, causing omission and commission errors) are overlapping manifestations of automation-induced effects with attention central, arising from interaction of personal, situational and automation-related factors. Complacency arises with multitasking where manual work competes with the automated task for attention, appears in novices and experts, and is not removed by simple practice. Bias is not prevented by training or instructions and affects individuals and teams. Goddard et al.: decision support usually improves overall performance but wrong advice can introduce new errors; automation bias frequency, mediators and mitigators were reviewed (see figures).
headline_figures: Goddard et al.: 13,821 papers retrieved, 74 included. Pooled analysis of four studies: risk ratio 1.26 (95% CI 1.11 to 1.44) for following erroneous CDSS advice vs control (about 26% higher risk of an incorrect decision). 'Negative consultations' (correct initial decision changed to incorrect after advice) roughly 6% to 11% across studies. All via summary, not verified in full text [uncertain]. Parasuraman and Manzey report no single headline number in the abstract.
sample_unit_and_population: Parasuraman and Manzey: review of empirical studies across aviation, process control and decision-support settings, with novices and experts [uncertain on study count]. Goddard et al.: 74 included papers, mostly clinical decision support and healthcare users; pooled meta-analysis of four studies.
observed_vs_stated: Mostly observed behaviour in experimental and simulated tasks (decisions following advice, monitoring performance). Self-reported trust is a mediator, not the main outcome. Individual study mix not verified [uncertain].
what_makes_trust_justified: Neither source gives a simple rule. What the abstracts and review say shapes calibrated reliance: Goddard et al. mitigators are training, emphasising user accountability (internal accountability worked better than external pressure in one study), displaying updated confidence levels with advice, presenting information rather than commands, reducing on-screen detail, and not placing advice too prominently. Parasuraman and Manzey point to attention and the interplay of personal, situational and automation factors, and say practice and instructions alone are not enough.
what_it_costs: Not quantified in either source. Implied costs: users must keep monitoring and do independent work alongside the aid, which is the workload the aid was meant to remove. Accountability and confidence displays add design and process effort.
failure_mode_class: Over-reliance: omission errors (missing a problem the aid did not flag) and commission errors (following wrong advice), plus complacent under-monitoring.
control_that_would_have_prevented: Not an incident study. Candidate controls from the review: confidence display, advice presented as information, user accountability, training. Workload and time pressure are named as aggravators (Goddard et al.: higher workload, task complexity, time pressure; user confidence and experience also mediate; less confident users more likely to accept advice).
limitations_stated: Not read in full text, so authors' stated limitations are not captured [uncertain]. Parasuraman and Manzey frame the model as a framework for future research, not a tested one. Goddard et al. flag that automation bias overlaps with complacency and that study designs vary [uncertain].
counter_evidence: Goddard et al.: most studies found decision support improved overall performance despite new errors, so aids net help when reliable. Evidence is from clinical and aviation-style tasks, not code review or LLM agents. Goddard et al.'s one-study finding on internal accountability is thin evidence.
verification_status: Parasuraman and Manzey abstract claims: checked against repository abstract summary only, full text not opened [uncertain]. Goddard et al. figures (74 of 13,821; RR 1.26; 6-11%): from PMC page via summariser, not confirmed in the paper text [uncertain]. Funding statement: quoted from the PMC fetch.
usable_claim: Research on automation in aviation and clinical decision support finds that people tend to over-rely on automated aids, following wrong advice and monitoring less, and that simple practice or instructions do not remove this. In a systematic review of clinical decision support, erroneous advice was followed more often than in controls, and higher workload and time pressure made it more likely.
do_not_use: Do not apply the 1.26 risk ratio or the 6-11% range to AI coding agents or code review. Do not quote wording as verbatim until the PDFs are opened. Do not claim that training cannot help at all (Goddard lists training as a mitigator).
